ety.text: From Middle English degre, borrowed from Old French degré (French: degré), itself from Latin gradus, with the prefix de-.

senses.d: A completed curriculum of study in tertiary education.
ex: She has two bachelor's degrees and is studying towards a master's degree.

senses.d: A unit of measurement of angle equal to ¹⁄₃₆₀ of a circle's circumference.
ex: A right angle is a ninety-degree angle.
Most humans have a field of vision of almost 180 degrees.

senses.d: A unit of measurement of temperature on any of several scales, such as Celsius or Fahrenheit.
ex: 212 degrees Fahrenheit is equal to 100 degrees Celsius.

senses.d: The sum of the exponents of a term; the order of a polynomial.
ex: A quadratic polynomial is a polynomial of degree 2.

senses.d: The dimensionality of a field extension.
ex: The set of complex numbers constitutes a field extension of degree 2 over the real numbers.
The Galois field #92;operatorname#123;GF#125;(125)#61;#92;operatorname#123;GF#125;(5³) has degree 3 over its subfield #92;operatorname#123;GF#125;(5).

senses.d: The number of edges that a vertex takes part in; a valency.
The number of logical connectives in a formula.
The curvature of a circular arc, expressed as the angle subtended by a fixed length of arc or chord.
A unit of measurement of latitude and longitude which together identify a location on the Earth's surface.
Any of the stages (like positive, comparative, superlative, elative) in the comparison of an adjective or an adverb.
